ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly calibrates historical ring-current theories against quantum chemical calculations, specifically benchmarking Johnson & Bovey’s 1958 equivalent-loop model and Haigh & Mallion’s 1980 current-density surface-integral model to update empirical intensity factors originally tabulated by Giessner-Prettre and Pullman. It applies these models to predict and interpret secondary magnetic shielding shifts for aromatic side chains in proteins and nucleic acids.
CITES: Johnson & Bovey 1958; Haigh & Mallion 1980; Giessner-Prettre & Pullman 1969; Buckingham 1960

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly tests and compares the Johnson-Bovey equivalent-loop model and Haigh-Mallion quantum mechanical current-density model to predict out-of-plane proton chemical shifts in [10]-paracyclophane. It historically evaluates the Johnson-Bovey two-loop separation parameter, finding a single loop at the ring plane provides the best fit, and documents a systematic intensity factor difference between the two foundational theories.
CITES: Pople 1956; Waugh & Fessenden 1957; Johnson & Bovey 1958; McWeeny 1958; Haigh & Mallion 1971

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper’s predictive framework explicitly incorporates the Haigh-Mallion current-density model to compute aromatic ring-current contributions to methyl shielding. It treats ring-current effects as a primary theoretical kernel, drawing on established calibration practices such as those detailed by Case (1995).
CITES: Case-1995

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The review traces the historical origin of the ring-current model to Pople (1956) and explains how circulating pi-electron currents generate secondary magnetic fields that modulate NMR shielding. It emphasizes that diatropic and paratropic responses are external-field-dependent phenomena, and in polycyclic systems, complex shielding patterns often arise from competing, counter-rotating currents rather than a single aromatic loop. These magnetic responses are subsequently evaluated through various computational proxies like NICS and ICSS.
CITES: Pople-1956

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper extends the Johnson-Bovey equivalent-loop model (1958) from isotropic shifts to the full chemical shielding anisotropy tensor, deriving a closed-form expression for the off-diagonal component. It benchmarks this ring-current kernel against DFT and protein NMR data, explicitly treating the Johnson-Bovey formulation as the foundational historical framework for calculating aromatic pi-electron ring-current effects on shielding.
CITES: Johnson-Bovey 1958; Haigh-Mallion 1971; Haigh-Mallion 1980; Sitkoff-Case 1998

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly benchmarks the classical empirical theories of aromatic ring-current shielding—the point-dipole formulation (Pople, 1956/1958), the equivalent-current-loop model (Johnson and Bovey, 1958), and the anisotropic current-density approach (Haigh and Mallion, 1980)—against quantum mechanical calculations of amide-proton shifts. It evaluates how these historical parameterizations predict secondary magnetic field effects from nearby aromatic residues and compares their predictive accuracy in modern chemical-shift modeling. The study finds that while all three rooted models achieve low RMSDs, a simple point-dipole approximation matches the more complex Johnson-Bovey and Haigh-Mallion formulations when parameters are refit.
CITES: Pople 1956/1958; Johnson and Bovey 1958; Haigh and Mallion 1980

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The review traces the historical roots of magnetic aromaticity diagnostics to Pople’s 1956 point-dipole ring current model and Pauling–Wheland’s 1933 work on diamagnetic susceptibility, establishing circulating π-electron currents as the physical mechanism for diatropic/paratropic NMR shielding effects. It discusses how these classical models underpin the interpretation of ¹H-NMR chemical shifts in annulene probes and later computational proxies like NICS, emphasizing how tensor decomposition isolates the π-ring-current contribution.
CITES: Pople 1956; Pauling-Wheland 1933; Schleyer 1996; Lazzeretti 2000; Mitchell 2001

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The review comprehensively traces the historical development of ring-current theory from Pauling and London through Pople, McWeeny, and Haigh-Mallion, evaluating how induced pi-electron circulations generate secondary magnetic fields that modify NMR chemical shielding and proton shifts. It contrasts semiempirical ring-current models with modern current-density calculations and ab initio shielding computations, emphasizing that ring-current corrections are practical interpretive tools rather than direct observables.
CITES: Pauling; London; Pople; McWeeny; Haigh and Mallion 1979/1980; Lazzeretti 2000; Schleyer et al. 1996; Fowler and Steiner

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper focuses on carbonyl magnetic anisotropy but cites Pople’s ring-current arguments in the introduction to establish the historical and theoretical lineage of magnetic shielding models. It positions its point-dipole parameterization within the broader mid-century effort to interpret chemical shifts via bond and ring anisotropy frameworks.
CITES: Pople

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper cites the Johnson-Bovey equivalent-loop model and Haigh-Mallion current-density theory as established historical frameworks for the secondary magnetic field of aromatic ring currents, using them to ground its grid-based visualization of through-space shielding.
CITES: Johnson-Bovey; Haigh-Mallion

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The ProCS15 predictor incorporates aromatic ring currents as an additive term to model isotropic shieldings for protein backbone and Cβ atoms. Rather than deriving or reviewing the foundational ring-current theories or their historical development, the authors parameterize the effect alongside hydrogen-bonding and conformational terms within their DFT-derived additive kernel.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper incorporates ring-current effects as explicit physical-chemical parameters within its ensemble-averaged chemical shift predictor, identifying them alongside magnetic anisotropy as the dominant terms for methyl-proton shifts. It applies these effects empirically to parameterize predictions against molecular dynamics trajectories, without engaging with the foundational point-dipole, equivalent-loop, or current-density models that historically explain the secondary magnetic field.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper centrally investigates how induced pi-electron currents in aromatic and antiaromatic systems generate measurable chemical shifts, calibrating the effect across annulenes and fused arenes. It frames the physical origin in the induced diatropic/paratropic magnetic field and emphasizes geometric constraints on shielding, focusing on empirical calibration and bond-localization correlations rather than detailing classical point-dipole or current-density shielding models.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly compares three foundational ring-current models for predicting protein ¹H chemical shifts: the classical point-dipole approximation (originating from Pople, 1956), the Johnson-Bovey equivalent-loop model (1958), and the Haigh-Mallion current-density model (1971/1980). It reparameterizes the point-dipole proportionality constant against a large experimental dataset and benchmarks it against the Johnson-Bovey and Haigh-Mallion estimates to refine the geometric factor used in NMR-constrained structure optimization.
CITES: Pople 1956; Haigh and Mallion 1971; Haigh and Mallion 1980; Johnson and Bovey 1958; Pauling 1936; Perkins and Dwek 1980

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper invokes aromatic ring-current shielding as the physical mechanism to explain extreme upfield NMR chemical shifts in the designed Trp-cage fold, citing Case’s SHIFTS code for quantitative correlation. It treats the effect as an established diagnostic fingerprint for fold validation and does not explore the historical roots, origin, or foundational theoretical models (e.g., point-dipole or equivalent-loop approximations) of the phenomenon.
CITES: Case

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: Pauling (1979) extends the ring-current concept to a non-aromatic system by modeling the peptide bond’s resonance-stabilized electrons as a circulating current analogous to aromatic pi-electrons. Grounding this in his 1936 theory of induced ring currents, he benchmarks the model against benzene to establish a historical bridge between aromatic ring-current shielding and amide-group diamagnetic anisotropy in proteins.
CITES: Pauling-1936; Lonsdale-1939; Worcester-1978

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly models the secondary magnetic field from circulating π-electrons using a differential Biot-Savart formulation, tracing the theory back to the standard integral Biot-Savart approach and classical ring-current concepts. It explicitly cites Haigh & Mallion (1971) and Lazzeretti (2000) as foundational accounts that established the current-density formalism and shielding-density decomposition. By decomposing the induced field into near- and far-ring volume elements, it demonstrates how historical point-dipole and loop approximations evolved into modern ab initio spatial maps that predict aromatic deshielding and shielding patterns.
CITES: Haigh & Mallion 1971; Lazzeretti 2000

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper directly applies and compares ring-current theories, explicitly adopting the Johnson–Bovey (1958) equivalent-loop model while rejecting the Haigh–Mallion (1971) current-density method due to its theoretical breakdown above the ring plane. It grounds its computational framework in the historical progression of these models, incorporating Giessner-Prettre and Pullman’s scaling factors to adapt benzene-normalized equations to aromatic amino acid systems.
CITES: Johnson and Bovey (1958); Haigh and Mallion (1971); Giessner-Prettre and Pullman (1969)

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper motivates its full tensor visualization method by explaining how circulating pi-electron ring currents and competing through-space currents generate directional shielding that scalar NICS averages obscure. It contrasts this physical mechanism with induced current-density maps, demonstrating that tensor eigenvalues isolate the competing aromatic and antiaromatic current pathways driving chemical shift variations.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper incorporates ring-current terms as a computational feature in its machine-learning framework and identifies ring-current shielding as a physical factor that shapes observed chemical shifts alongside hydrogen bonding and rotamer effects. It treats these contributions empirically as model descriptors and ensemble observables, without addressing the theoretical origins or historical development of aromatic current models.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper interprets observed cysteine thiol chemical shifts by factoring in their spatial proximity to nearby aromatic residues and the associated ring-current shielding, treating the phenomenon as a practical interpretive constraint rather than an isolated structural readout. It applies this effect for assignment validation but does not engage with the theoretical models or historical origins of aromatic current effects.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper incorporates a point-dipole ring current correction, expressed as (1−3cos²θ)/r³, into its CamShift shift prediction kernel to model aromatic shielding. It explicitly traces this magnetic susceptibility model to Pople (1958), using the classical point-dipole formalism to parameterize through-space distance dependencies in its MD restraint pipeline.
CITES: Pople 1958

ENGAGES: deals-with
HOW: The paper centrally compares three foundational ring-current models—Pople’s 1956 point-dipole, the Waugh–Fessenden–Johnson–Bovey equivalent-loop current approaches (1957/1958), and Haigh–Mallion’s 1972/1980 Hückel surface-integral method—to quantify their contributions to RNA base chemical shifts. It establishes a unified sign convention across these historically distinct formulations and derives empirical interconversion equations to reconcile their geometric factors.
CITES: Pople 1956; Waugh and Fessenden 1957; Johnson and Bovey 1958; Haigh and Mallion 1972; Haigh and Mallion 1980

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper introduces NICS as a ring-center magnetic shielding metric to probe aromaticity, explicitly connecting shielding response to ring-current language and citing Pople and Untch (1966) on ring-current shifts as historical context for magnetic aromaticity criteria.
CITES: Pople and Untch 1966

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper treats ring-current effects as an established empirical correction term added to database-driven shift predictions, noting that these secondary magnetic field contributions are computationally difficult to derive from first principles and depend critically on the precise coordinates of aromatic side chains.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-intro
HOW: The paper treats ring-current effects as an established empirical descriptor, citing Case (1995) for the underlying calibration framework, and does not address the historical development or physical models of aromatic pi-electron circulation. It incorporates the effect purely as a fixed structural input feature within its neural-network shift predictor.
CITES: Case 1995

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper incorporates ring-current effects as a distinct physical term for interpreting proton shielding in peptides, citing Case 1995 for ring-current calibration. It positions these aromatic pi-electron secondary fields alongside electric-field and bond anisotropy terms within a broader geometric decomposition of chemical shifts.
CITES: Case 1995; Osapay and Case 1991; Williamson and Asakura 1993

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper treats ring-current effects as a secondary, longer-range interaction that provides context for aromatic tensor shifts rather than developing its own ring-current theory. It acknowledges the foundational historical models by explicitly pointing to Johnson-Bovey (1958) for the equivalent-loop approach and Haigh-Mallion (1980) for current-density calculations as key references for the field.
CITES: Johnson-Bovey 1958; Haigh-Mallion 1980

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The authors attribute observed upfield proton shifts in Z-DNA to base ring-current effects, noting that carbon-13 shifts do not follow the same directional trend. This brief discussion links conformational changes to magnetic shielding variations without invoking specific theoretical models or historical frameworks.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper briefly addresses aromatic ring currents as a potential dominant contributor to secondary chemical shifts, framing them alongside hydrogen bonding and macrodipoles as environmental terms influencing shielding. It references earlier ring-current calibration studies to contextualize how shift data should be interpreted and cross-validated against structural databases.
CITES: Szilagyi and Jardetzky 1989; Pastore and Saudek 1990; Pardi/Wagner/Wuthrich 1983; Wuthrich 1986

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The paper notes that aromatic side chains (approximated as benzene rings) generate diamagnetic anisotropy that competes with peptide-plane contributions, and that protein magnetic orientation measurements remain sensitive to aromatic-ring orientation. It frames this aromatic anisotropy as a distinct physical mechanism that must be separated from backbone effects when interpreting magnetic susceptibility data.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The authors mention ring-current effects only once in their concluding discussion, cautioning that their sequence-only machine learning model should not be taken as evidence that physical shielding contributions such as ring currents can be discarded from chemical shift theories.
CITES: none

ENGAGES: touches-discussion
HOW: The authors qualitatively attribute an upfield methoxy chemical shift to aromatic ring-current shielding to corroborate the assigned trans geometry of the photodimer, using the effect strictly as supporting structural evidence without elaborating on its theoretical models or historical development.
CITES: none
